common_name: Nancy Hall Sweet Potato (Moist Southern Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm, in loose, well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; Nancy Hall is an old Deep South dooryard heirloom grown for its exceptionally moist, sweet flesh.

directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil formed into ridges in full sun; Nancy Hall is a Deep South heirloom variety grown since the early 20th century for pale copper-pink skinned tubers with soft, exceptionally moist, deep-orange flesh that cooks up custardy rather than dry or mealy, a texture many older Southern gardeners still prefer to modern commercial types like Beauregard. Vines are long and vigorous and tubers form somewhat irregularly shaped, so hill soil up generously and harvest carefully to avoid bruising the tender skin. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall, before the first frost, and cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for one to two weeks to firm the skin, heal nicks, and sweeten the flesh before storing.

common_name: Bunch Porto Rico Sweet Potato (Compact Vintage Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2–4 weeks after last frost in well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; the compact, semi-bush vine habit takes noticeably less room to sprawl than most heirloom sweet potatoes, making it a better fit for smaller garden beds.

directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil formed into ridges in full sun; Bunch Porto Rico is an early-20th-century American selection from the old Porto Rico sweet potato line, valued for a more compact, semi-bush vining habit that spreads far less aggressively than standard long-vine heirlooms, making it practical for gardeners short on space. It produces copper-skinned tubers with moist, deep-orange, sweet flesh similar in eating quality to its Porto Rico parent, and its shorter vines are easier to manage, hill, and keep out of walkways through the growing season. Dig tubers once the vines begin to yellow and before frost threatens, then cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to heal cuts and concentrate sweetness before storage.
